nodes.label: Pipeline tracker
nodes.one_line: Keep a live list of every opportunity with status, deadline, and owner so you always know what's in flight and what's due.
know_what: pipeline statuses — the shared stage vocabulary (research → LOI → full proposal → awarded → declined) that makes any row readable at a glance
owner per row — the single person accountable for each opportunity's next action
next action — the one concrete step, dated, that moves a row to the next status
aging — how long an opportunity has sat in one status; rows stuck 30+ days are the first sign of a broken pipeline
conversion ratio — the pipeline arithmetic (submissions vs awards) used to sanity-check revenue forecasts
single source of truth — the rule that the tracker, not anyone's memory, is where opportunity state lives
know_how: create one row per opportunity with status, deadline, owner, ask amount, and source portal
advance a row only when its next action completes — a status change is an event, not an edit
review the pipeline weekly with each row's owner and rewrite next actions in that session
log every declined decision with its date and reason so the tracker carries history, not just inventory
run a monthly aging report and force a decision on every row stuck 30+ days in one status
keep the tracker in one tool the whole team uses (spreadsheet, Airtable, or a CRM such as Salesforce NPSP) so a second spreadsheet of truth never appears
habits: checking the pipeline before agreeing to any new work — capacity starts with what is already in flight
writing the next action and its date onto every row in the same session you touch it
treating a row without an owner as an uncommitted opportunity
updating the tracker the day a decision lands, not the day after
reviewing the tracker with the team weekly, not only when a deadline looms
nodes.checkpoint: Maintain a tracker with at least 10 live opportunities where every row has a status from the shared vocabulary, a dated deadline, and a named owner, and no row has sat 30+ days without a logged next action.
nodes.common_failure: Keeping the pipeline in one person's head or a private spreadsheet — the tracker dies at the first vacation or departure, and opportunities get missed because 'someone was handling it'.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
Candid — grant tracking and pipeline resources
GrantStation — prospect tracking guidance

nodes.label: Portfolio goals
nodes.one_line: Set a revenue target and funder mix for the year so individual proposals serve a portfolio, not a whim.
know_what: revenue target — the annual dollar amount grant-seeking must raise, split out from earned and committed income
funder mix — the intended split of that target across federal, foundation, corporate, and regranting sources
coverage gap — the difference between committed funding and the target, which is exactly what the pipeline must fill
portfolio goals vs single-ask goals — what one proposal must win vs what the year must raise
conversion-based pipeline volume — the asks needed to hit the target given your win rate (a 30% win rate implies 3-4x the target in submissions)
multi-year view — how this year's target connects to next year's already-committed vs still-to-raise revenue
know_how: derive the revenue target from the operating budget: what grants must cover after earned income and committed funds
set the funder mix by reverse-engineering from current sources — what each type gives today and what share you want it to become
estimate the pipeline volume the target implies using your conversion ratio before committing to the number
break the annual target into quarterly sub-targets aligned to the funding calendar's cycles
write the goals down where the pipeline tracker lives so every new opportunity is evaluated against them
review targets against actuals quarterly and re-forecast, not just at year end
habits: asking 'what does this year need to raise' before 'what should we apply for'
rechecking the mix whenever one source surprises — a big loss or a big award changes the goal
keeping the revenue target visible wherever proposals are discussed
testing each new opportunity against the mix: does it serve the goal or only the moment
reviewing targets against actuals monthly rather than annually
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a written annual revenue target with a funder-mix split, the coverage gap in dollars, and the pipeline volume implied by your conversion ratio.
nodes.common_failure: Setting a target after the year is half over, or setting one number with no mix — the portfolio drifts toward whatever funder is easiest that month and the year ends with the wrong revenue shape.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
Nonprofit Finance Fund — sustainability and revenue planning
Beverly Browning, Grant Writing For Dummies

nodes.label: Win/loss debrief
nodes.one_line: Debrief every decision — win, loss, no-decision — and extract the pattern that improves your next ask.
know_what: win/loss debrief — the structured review of every decision once the funder responds: win, loss, or no-decision
reviewer comments — the written scores and narrative feedback federal agencies return (e.g., NIH summary statements) and foundations rarely volunteer
no-decision — the silent pass (never invited to full proposal, never contacted), logged as its own outcome
decision log — the running record of outcomes and reasons that turns individual losses into portfolio data
outcome coding — bucketing each decision into fit, relationship, budget, competition, or craft so patterns become countable
debrief cadence — the rule that every decision is reviewed within days, while memory is fresh
know_how: request reviewer comments when the funder does not volunteer them — many foundations will share on request
run the debrief within a week of the decision: what worked, what did not, what you would change
enter the outcome and named reason into the decision log before starting the next proposal
code every loss into the same buckets so cross-proposal patterns become countable
look for patterns quarterly: losses concentrating in one funder type, one ask size, or one season
hand the debrief to the next writer of that funder's proposal so the lesson travels
habits: debriefing losses promptly instead of letting them go quiet
asking for feedback even on wins — 'what nearly lost us this one'
coding every outcome into the same buckets so patterns can be counted
checking the decision log before writing any new proposal for what this funder or type already taught you
treating a declined proposal as data, not failure
nodes.checkpoint: Run a debrief within a week of a funder decision and enter the outcome, the named reason, and one change for the next ask into the decision log, quoting reviewer comments when available.
nodes.common_failure: Debriefing only losses (or only wins), so the pattern comes out skewed — or holding the debrief so long after the decision that the record reads 'can't remember' and the lesson evaporates.
sources: NIH — summary statement and review criteria guidance
The Grantsmanship Center Magazine — post-decision debrief discussions
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need

nodes.label: Prospecting rhythm
nodes.one_line: Run a weekly scan-and-log habit so new funders enter the pipeline continuously instead of in deadline-driven panics.
know_what: scan-and-log — the weekly ritual of checking saved searches and alerts, then logging anything new into the tracker in the same sitting
Grants.gov email alerts — saved-search notifications that fire when a new opportunity matches your keywords
Candid search templates — saved Foundation Directory searches re-run weekly to catch new or changed foundation records
state and local portals — state grant databases and regional funder sites with their own alert systems
lead time — the weeks a funder needs from first contact to LOI, which the rhythm must build in
deadline-driven panic — the failure mode where prospecting happens only when a deadline forces it
know_how: set up Grants.gov saved searches with email alerts for your top three program keywords
build and save 3-5 Candid search templates (subject, geography, population) and re-run them on a fixed weekday
block a weekly 30-60 minute prospecting slot on the same day every week
log every new opportunity into the tracker with status 'research' in the same session you find it
triage each find against the revenue target and funder mix before it becomes a pipeline candidate
refresh the saved searches quarterly as keywords and priorities drift
habits: prospecting on a schedule, not when a gap appears
logging a find the same day it is found — unlogged research is lost research
keeping the weekly slot even when the pipeline is full, because the pipeline always empties
noting why each find passed or failed triage so the search templates sharpen
checking alerts at a fixed time and clearing them to zero
nodes.checkpoint: Complete a full weekly scan — Grants.gov alerts, Candid templates, and state portals — and log every new opportunity into the tracker with a status and a triage note, for four consecutive weeks.
nodes.common_failure: Prospecting in bursts — a quarterly scramble before a deadline — so the pipeline is feast-or-famine and the funder mix is whatever was urgent, not what was planned.
sources: Grants.gov — saved searches and email alerts
Candid Foundation Directory — saved search templates
Beverly Browning, Grant Writing For Dummies

nodes.label: Funding calendar
nodes.one_line: Build a 12-month calendar of recurring deadlines and submission windows so you plan proposals in seasons, not sprints.
know_what: recurring deadlines — the annual cycles many funders run, same month every year (e.g., many state agencies' March windows)
submission windows — the open periods (Grants.gov NOFOs typically open 60-90 days) inside which all work must fit
board-meeting cycles — foundations that decide at quarterly board meetings, so LOIs must land 2-4 months ahead
12-month rolling calendar — the forward view showing every known deadline and window for the year
internal milestone buffer — the lead time before submission your own review needs, commonly two weeks for federal
seasonal clustering — the tendency of deadlines to bunch (federal fall cycles, foundation spring cycles) that the calendar must expose
know_how: collect every known deadline from the tracker, funder websites, and prior award cycles into one calendar
record each deadline twice: the submission date and the internal milestone (draft done, review done) two weeks earlier
mark recurring cycles with their historical months drawn from prior years' NOFOs or the foundation's pattern
work backward from each deadline to the draft start date so the calendar shows when writing must begin
review the 12-month view monthly and update it as new NOFOs drop
color-code by pipeline (federal / foundation / corporate) so the year's mix is visible at a glance
habits: checking the calendar before committing to any new opportunity's timeline
adding a deadline to the calendar the same week it is discovered
looking at the next 90 days weekly, not just this month
watching for clusters and deliberately not starting a new sprint inside one
keeping the calendar in the same tool as the tracker so the two never disagree
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a 12-month calendar with every known recurring deadline and submission window, internal milestones marked two weeks before each submission date, and the next 90 days free of conflicting proposal sprints.
nodes.common_failure: A calendar holding only the deadlines you remembered — the recurring cycles not yet announced are missing, so the year's plan collapses when a NOFO lands in the middle of another sprint.
sources: Grants.gov — forecast and current opportunities
Candid — funding calendar features
Foundation websites' 'apply' pages and board-cycle announcements

nodes.label: Capacity planning
nodes.one_line: Match the pipeline to the hours you actually have, and say no to opportunities you can't staff to a competitive standard.
know_what: hours-per-proposal costing — the real time by proposal type: 30-40 hours for a full federal narrative, 8-10 for a foundation LOI-plus-proposal
go/no-go — the explicit pre-drafting decision of whether an opportunity gets your scarce hours
capacity ceiling — the team's total proposal hours per quarter after program work, meetings, and reporting
competitive standard — the floor of effort below which a proposal should not be submitted at all
opportunity cost — the proposal you did not write well because you wrote three adequately
submission-quality floor — the reality that a thin proposal can damage your standing with a funder more than declining
know_how: compute the team's quarterly capacity: staff proposal hours minus meetings, reporting, and other commitments
estimate each pipeline opportunity's hours from type (LOI vs full federal proposal) before committing to it
run a go/no-go on every opportunity: hours required, odds, fit, and what it displaces
decline early and explicitly when over capacity, and log the decline so the funder is not left hanging
sequence the pipeline so high-hour federal proposals do not cluster in one quarter
re-forecast capacity whenever the pipeline changes by more than a couple of rows
habits: counting hours before counting dollars
treating a full pipeline as a reason to prune, not to work more
saying no to the funder's face rather than silently underbidding
reviewing the capacity math quarterly against actual hours spent
keeping the costing numbers honest by tracking actual hours per proposal type
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a quarterly capacity plan listing every pipeline opportunity with estimated hours, each marked go/no-go with a reason, and total hours within the team's ceiling.
nodes.common_failure: Saying yes to everything because 'it's free money' — the team spreads across ten undercooked proposals, loses most of them, and damages the very relationships it had capacity to serve well.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
The Grantsmanship Center Magazine — go/no-go and capacity discussions
Beverly Browning, Grant Writing For Dummies

nodes.label: Revenue diversification
nodes.one_line: Shape the portfolio so no single funder or funding type is load-bearing for your budget.
know_what: concentration risk — the share of budget carried by one funder; no single funder above 25-30% of budget is the common rule of thumb
funding-type mix — the balance across federal, foundation, corporate, and earned revenue, each with different cycles and rules
funder concentration — dependence on one relationship whose priorities, calendar, or giving cap become your binding constraint
co-termination risk — the danger of several large grants ending in the same year and leaving a revenue cliff
replacement cost — the lead time to replace a lost funder, commonly 6-18 months, which concentration ignores
portfolio shape — the intended distribution of revenue across funders and types that the tracker and goals are meant to enforce
know_how: compute the concentration ratio — largest funder's share of total budget — and flag anything above 25-30%
map the portfolio by funder type and by grant end-date to expose co-termination cliffs
set a diversification target inside the annual goals, e.g., no single type more than 50% of grant revenue
use the win/loss log and the prospecting rhythm to open new funder types deliberately, before a loss forces it
plan replacements 12-18 months out for any funder above the concentration threshold
rebalance the mix quarterly against actuals, adjusting prospecting and goal-setting
habits: asking 'what is our largest funder's share' quarterly, before it becomes a surprise
treating a single 40% funder as an emergency, not a win
recruiting new funder types when the mix tilts, not when a grant ends
checking grant end-dates together, not one at a time
keeping the concentration number on the dashboard next to the revenue target

know_why.claim: Diversify grant revenue across funder types so no single funder or funding type is load-bearing for the budget.
know_why.because: funder priorities, budgets, and cycles shift without notice; a funder above roughly 25-30% of budget makes its annual decision existential, and the 6-18 month replacement lead time means the loss lands before the pipeline can recover.
know_why.disputed_by: cultivation-school practitioners who argue the returns are deepest when you double down on the few funder relationships that already work, and that spreading thin across types produces a portfolio of shallow, low-odds asks.
know_why.source: Nonprofit Finance Fund — sustainability planning guidance; the concentration-vs-cultivation debate runs in The Grantsmanship Center Magazine

nodes.checkpoint: Compute your largest funder's share of the annual budget, map every grant end-date, and produce a written plan that brings any funder above 25-30% below the threshold within 18 months.
nodes.common_failure: Treating the biggest funder as the safest — concentration feels like success until that funder's priorities pivot, and the 6-18 month replacement lead time becomes a budget crisis that diversification would have spread across.
sources: Nonprofit Finance Fund — sustainability and revenue-mix guidance
The Grantsmanship Center Magazine — portfolio diversification debates
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
